title: The Geometry of the Three Cases
quickIdea: Two unknowns give lines and three give planes, and the rank pair tells you which arrangement you are looking at: crossing, parallel, coincident, a common line, or a triangular prism.
remember: Two unknowns: a unique solution means two lines crossing at a point; no solution means parallel distinct lines; infinitely many means the same line written twice.

Three unknowns, coefficient rank r and augmented rank s: r = s = 3 is a single point, r = s = 2 is a common line, r = s = 1 is one plane written three times, r = 2 with s = 3 is a triangular prism with no common point, r = 1 with s = 2 is three parallel planes.
The prism case is the one that fools the eye: every pair of planes meets in a line, yet the three lines are different and there is no common point.
In the column picture the same cases read as: b inside a 3-dimensional span (unique), inside a 2-dimensional span (a line of solutions), or outside the span (no solution).
Geometry is a check, not a method: the rank pair is what the answer is graded on.

example.prompt: Describe the solution set of x + y = 1, 2x + 2y = 2 geometrically and by rank.
example.work: The second equation is twice the first, so both are the same line. A = [[1,1],[2,2]] has rank 1, and [A|b] = [[1,1,1],[2,2,2]] also has rank 1, with n = 2.
example.answer: One line, so infinitely many solutions: rank(A) = rank([A|b]) = 1 < 2, one free parameter. Replacing b by (1,3) makes the lines parallel and distinct, rank([A|b]) becomes 2 and there is no solution.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 1998 Q.1.2 is the parallel case in three unknowns, GATE CSE 2025 Set 1 Q.13 turns the geometric split into a statement about k, and GATE CSE 2003 Q.41 asks for the parameter that makes the planes share a line.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Three planes in R^3 pairwise intersect in three different lines. How many solutions has the system?
variations.why: That is the prism case, rank(A) = 2 with rank([A|b]) = 3, so the system is inconsistent even though every pair of equations is solvable.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Two lines in the plane are given by equations with proportional left-hand sides and proportional right-hand sides. What does the system look like?
variations.answer: One line written twice, so infinitely many solutions.
variations.why: Proportional rows make rank(A) = 1, and proportional constants keep rank([A|b]) = 1 as well.

trap.what: Judging the number of solutions from a sketch of the row picture when the system has more than three unknowns, or treating pairwise intersection as a common intersection.
trap.why: The row picture is only drawable up to three unknowns, and pairwise consistency is strictly weaker than joint consistency.
trap.counterexample: x + y + z = 1, x - y + z = 1, 2x + 2z = 3: any two of them meet in a line, and yet rank(A) = 2 while rank([A|b]) = 3, so the three have no common point.

check.question: A 3-unknown system has rank(A) = 2 and rank([A|b]) = 2. What does the solution set look like?
check.explanation: Consistent with one free parameter, so the solutions form a line in R^3: the intersection of the planes is a common line.
